children.title: Trump names Michael Ellis CIA deputy director
children.description_medium: On February 3, 2025, President Donald Trump named Michael Ellis as CIA deputy director, a role that does not require Senate confirmation. Ellis, a lawyer and former aide to Representative Devin Nunes, was sworn in on February 10. His prior positions included NSA general counsel and senior director for intelligence programs at the National Security Council.
children.description_long: President Donald Trump named Michael Ellis as deputy director of the Central Intelligence Agency on February 3, 2025. The Washington Post reported that Ellis was a lawyer and former aide to Representative Devin Nunes, and noted that the deputy director position does not require Senate confirmation. The CIA later announced that Ellis was sworn in on February 10. These two supplied sources document the appointment and the subsequent oath of office, so the event chronology includes both dates while distinguishing the announcement from the swearing-in. Ellis had previously served as NSA general counsel and as a senior director for intelligence programs at the National Security Council, according to the appointment report. The available sources support describing his professional background and his appointment to a senior agency role. The “political ally” characterization appears in the reported context, but the sources do not establish that political loyalty rather than professional qualifications determined the selection. This record therefore states the documented appointment and background without asserting that the selection was improper or based solely on allegiance.
children.date_uncertainty: February 3 is the appointment announcement date; the CIA says Ellis was sworn in February 10, 2025.

children.title: Gabbard revokes clearances of 37 intelligence officials
children.description_medium: Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former intelligence officials, The Washington Post reported on August 19, 2025. The supplied correction identifies this as a discrete clearance action. It does not establish the original account’s broader claim that one investigation documented a combined purge across several agencies and specialist groups.
children.description_long: Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former intelligence officials, according to Washington Post reporting published August 19, 2025. The packet identifies this as a discrete action, separate from the appointment of Michael Ellis, the March probationary CIA dismissals and the May National Intelligence Council personnel changes. The supplied report supports the number of people whose clearances were revoked and the date of the announcement. It does not establish that the action formed part of a single personnel campaign spanning every agency or specialist category described in the original omnibus account. The source also does not establish the broad asserted motive that intelligence specialists were replaced by loyalists chosen through social-media activism. This event should therefore be represented as the clearance action reported by the newspaper, with its own date and institutional scope. The broader cumulative-purge narrative remains unsupported by the specific source record supplied for this task.
children.date_uncertainty: The date is the Washington Post publication and reported announcement date.

children.title: CIA removes senior Russia expert days after Alaska summit
children.description_medium: The Washington Post reported on August 27, 2025, that the Trump administration had removed the CIA’s senior-most Russia expert days after the Alaska summit. August 27 is the publication date; the packet dates the removal only relative to the summit. This action was reported separately from Gabbard’s August 19 revocation of 37 officials’ clearances.
children.description_long: The Washington Post reported on August 27, 2025, that the Trump administration had removed the CIA’s senior-most Russia expert days after the Alaska summit. The report treats the removal as a distinct personnel action in the intelligence community. It is separate from the August 19 announcement that Tulsi Gabbard revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former officials, even though both events appeared in reporting about changes affecting intelligence personnel. The supplied source supports the timing relative to the summit and the reported removal of the CIA official described as its senior-most Russia expert. It does not by itself establish that this removal was caused by the clearance action, that a single Washington Post investigation documented a combined purge across several agencies, or that the official was replaced by a political loyalist. The event is therefore limited to the reported removal and its chronology. Broader claims about the cumulative effect and motive require separate evidence beyond the source supplied here.
children.date_uncertainty: August 27 is the article publication date; the report dates the removal as occurring days after the Alaska summit.

unresolved_components.title: March probationary CIA dismissals and May NIC removals
unresolved_components.reason: The packet flags these proposed components for separate verification and contains no direct claims or source URLs for them.
unresolved_components.missing_evidence: Direct dated sources establishing the personnel actions, individuals affected, and responsible decision-makers.

unresolved_components.title: Omnibus loyalist-purge motive and cross-agency cumulative account
unresolved_components.reason: The packet says located reporting covers discrete actions and does not establish the broad replacement narrative or motive.
unresolved_components.missing_evidence: Source evidence tying the separate actions together and establishing the claimed selection rationale.

rationale: The supplied claims and sources support the Ellis appointment/sworn-in timeline and two distinct August events. Unverified March and May claims are explicitly left unresolved.

children.title: Acting DOJ leadership orders review of personnel tied to January 6 cases
children.description_medium: On January 31, 2025, acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove directed personnel actions and ordered the FBI to identify employees who had worked on January 6 investigations for review. The directives came before Kash Patel became FBI director. The FBI’s official biography dates Patel’s start to February 20, distinguishing the acting DOJ leadership’s actions from his later tenure.
children.description_long: Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove directed personnel actions at the Justice Department and ordered the FBI to identify employees who had worked on January 6 investigations for review, Reuters reported on January 31, 2025. This occurred before Kash Patel became FBI director. The FBI’s official biography gives Patel’s start date as February 20, 2025, so the January actions cannot accurately be attributed to Patel acting in that role. The supplied reporting supports the chronology and Bove’s responsibility for the directives described. It does not establish the original entry’s claim that Patel personally removed at least 75 career lawyers and FBI officials in his first month. The review request and personnel actions should be described as events under acting DOJ leadership, preserving the distinction between Bove’s January direction and Patel’s later tenure. This record does not infer how many employees were ultimately removed or the outcome of the review because the source material here does not establish those totals or results.
children.date_uncertainty: January 31 is the Reuters publication date and reported date of the directive; Patel’s official start date as FBI director was February 20.

children.title: FBI under Patel expands polygraph use in leak investigations
children.description_medium: By April 28, 2025, the FBI was using polygraph examinations in leak investigations at Director Kash Patel’s direction, according to a bureau spokesperson quoted by The Washington Post. Later reporting described some senior personnel being asked whether they had disparaged Patel. April 28 is the article’s publication date; the supplied material gives no single start date for the practice.
children.description_long: The FBI began using polygraph examinations as part of leak investigations under Director Kash Patel, according to Washington Post reporting published April 28, 2025. The newspaper reported that an FBI spokesperson confirmed Patel had directed the use of polygraphs in those investigations. Later reporting described some senior personnel being asked whether they had disparaged Patel. This is a distinct practice introduced under Patel’s leadership, separate from personnel-review directives issued by acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove before Patel became FBI director. The evidence in the packet supports the bureau’s reported use of polygraphs in leak hunts and the attributed detail about questions to some senior employees. It does not show that every FBI employee was tested, establish the total number of examinations, or substantiate a broad aggregate count of officials removed by Patel. The account is limited to the policy and reported application described by the newspaper, rather than treating separate personnel and investigative actions as one purge.
children.date_uncertainty: April 28 is the Washington Post publication date; the report describes the FBI’s use of polygraphs under Patel without specifying a single start date.

children.title: FBI plans to move up to 1,500 headquarters staff and agents
children.description_medium: FBI managers were told on February 21, 2025, that up to 1,500 employees would be moved from headquarters to field offices as Kash Patel began his tenure. The plan was presented as shifting resources toward field operations. The supplied reporting does not establish that all transfers occurred or that the purpose was to force attrition.
children.description_long: FBI managers were told that up to 1,500 employees would be moved from headquarters to field offices, The Washington Post reported on February 21, 2025. The plan emerged as Kash Patel began his tenure as FBI director and was presented as a rebalancing toward field operations. The supplied report describes a planned transfer of staff and agents; it does not establish that all 1,500 moves were completed or that the purpose was to force employees to leave the bureau. This transfer plan is a separate management action from the January personnel review directed by acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove and the later polygraph use reported under Patel. The original record combined these events and attributed them collectively to Patel’s confirmation, but the dates and actors differ. This description preserves the reported maximum number, the planned destination of the transfers, and the agency’s stated operational framing without treating a plan as a completed mass removal.
children.date_uncertainty: February 21 is the Washington Post publication date; the source describes managers being told of the plan around Patel’s start.

unresolved_components.title: Claim that Patel removed at least 75 officials in his first month
unresolved_components.reason: The packet identifies the aggregate count as unverified and the January actions predated Patel’s tenure.
unresolved_components.missing_evidence: A sourced, dated count with clear inclusion criteria and evidence attributing those removals to Patel.

rationale: The packet supports three distinct events involving different dates and actors. The descriptions distinguish acting DOJ leadership from Patel’s later FBI tenure and preserve the transfer plan as a plan.

children.title: Trump declares a national emergency at the southern border
children.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued Proclamation 10886, titled “Declaring a National Emergency at the Southern Border of the United States.” The proclamation directed executive agencies to use specified authorities and resources for border enforcement. It did not itself invoke the Alien Enemies Act; that separate presidential action followed on March 15.
children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued Proclamation 10886, declaring a national emergency at the southern border of the United States. The official proclamation directed executive agencies to use specified authorities and resources for border enforcement. It is a discrete action with its own date and stated subject: a national emergency at the southern border. The proclamation did not itself invoke the Alien Enemies Act. The separate invocation of that statute against alleged members of Tren de Aragua came on March 15, nearly two months later, under another presidential proclamation. Keeping the two measures distinct avoids attributing the later statutory action to the January emergency declaration. The supplied GovInfo document is the primary record for the January action and supports its date, title, emergency declaration, and directions to agencies. This account reports the proclamation’s contents without adding claims about the legality or operational effect of authorities beyond what the text documents.
children.date_uncertainty: The date is the date of Proclamation 10886 as published in the official record.

children.title: Trump invokes Alien Enemies Act against alleged Tren de Aragua members
children.description_medium: On March 15, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation invoking the Alien Enemies Act against Venezuelan nationals he alleged were members of Tren de Aragua. The proclamation described the group as engaged in an invasion or predatory incursion. That characterization is the administration’s allegation, and the invocation was separate from the January 20 border emergency.
children.description_long: President Donald Trump issued a proclamation on March 15, 2025, invoking the Alien Enemies Act against Venezuelan nationals whom the administration alleged were members of Tren de Aragua. The proclamation described the group as engaged in an invasion or predatory incursion. The action is separate from Trump’s January 20 declaration of a national emergency at the southern border: that earlier proclamation did not itself invoke the Alien Enemies Act. The White House proclamation is the primary source supplied for the date, the statute invoked, the population to whom the action was directed, and the administration’s characterization of the group. That characterization is presented as the proclamation’s allegation rather than an independently established finding about every person covered. The record supports reporting the invocation as a discrete presidential action on March 15, not as part of the January 20 event. It does not make a separate determination about the legal validity or implementation of the proclamation.
children.date_uncertainty: The date is the date of the White House proclamation invoking the Act.

rationale: The official records support two presidential actions on separate dates. The January border emergency and March Alien Enemies Act invocation are not merged.
